definition: Having plenty of room inside; able to hold a large amount.
example: Her capacious memory held the birthday of every cousin in the family.
nuance: Capacious stresses how much something can hold, while spacious stresses open room to move around in.
prompt: A hiker is choosing a backpack for a week-long trip in the mountains.
options: She chose the capacious pack because it fit her tent, stove, and a week of food.
The capacious pack was so tiny that only a single water bottle would squeeze inside.
Her capacious mood about the hike swung from eager to gloomy every few hours.
She called the trail capacious because it climbed so steeply over loose rocks.
reasons: A pack that swallows a tent and a week of supplies clearly holds a great deal.
A bag that barely fits one bottle is cramped, the reverse of the word's meaning.
Sudden mood swings describe capricious, a look-alike; the word is about holding a lot.
Steepness and rocky ground say nothing about how much something can contain.

practice.prompt: A family is touring an old house they are thinking about buying.
options: The capacious landlord raised the rent on a whim and then lowered it the next week.
The capacious doorbell played a cheerful two-note chime whenever guests arrived.
The capacious pantry had enough shelves to store a whole season of canned beans.
The capacious closet was so narrow that one winter coat filled it completely.
reasons: Acting on whims fits capricious, a similar-sounding word, not one about room.
A doorbell's sound has nothing to do with interior space or holding things.
Shelving for months of food shows a room that can take in a large quantity.
A closet crammed full by a single coat has very little room, the opposite idea.
